Random access memory (RAM)
Cache memory
Registers inside the CPU

Why are GPUs well suited for training machine learning models?

They use spinning magnetic platters to store and retrieve data very rapidly
They execute the fetch-decode-execute cycle faster than any CPU core

The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. It repeatedly performs the
fetch-decode-execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it
means, and execute it. CPU speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz), billions of cycles
per second. Modern CPUs contain multiple cores, each capable of executing instructions
independently, which allows a computer to make progress on several tasks at once.

Computers use a hierarchy of storage that trades speed against capacity and cost.
Registers inside the CPU are the fastest and smallest. Cache memory sits next to the
CPU cores and holds recently used data. Random access memory (RAM) is the computer's
working memory: it holds running programs and their data, and its contents are lost
when power is removed — RAM is volatile. Persistent storage — solid-state drives (SSD)
and hard disk drives (HDD) — retains data without power. SSDs use flash memory with no
moving parts and are much faster than HDDs, which store data on spinning magnetic
platters.

The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects every component. Buses are the
communication pathways that carry data between the CPU, memory, and devices. The
chipset manages traffic between components. Expansion slots allow additional cards,
such as a dedicated graphics card, to be added.

Input devices bring data into the computer: keyboards, mice, touchscreens, cameras,
and microphones. Output devices present results: monitors, speakers, and printers.
Ports such as USB provide standardized connections for peripherals. Device drivers are
software components that let the operating system communicate with specific hardware.

The graphics processing unit (GPU) contains thousands of small cores designed to
perform many simple calculations simultaneously. GPUs were created to render images
and video, but their parallel design also makes them well suited to scientific
computing and training machine learning models.

In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip doubled
roughly every two years, an observation known as Moore's law. For decades this drove
exponential growth in computing power at falling cost. In recent years the pace has
slowed as transistors approach physical limits, pushing the industry toward multi-core
designs, specialized chips, and better software efficiency.

questions.question: What distinguishes a WAN from a LAN?
options: A WAN uses packet switching, while a LAN does not.
A WAN spans cities or continents, while a LAN covers a small area such as a home or office.
A WAN connects devices wirelessly, while a LAN uses only wired connections.
A WAN is limited to a single building, while a LAN spans multiple cities.

questions.question: What is the role of routers on the internet?
options: They translate domain names into IP addresses for browsers.
They split large files into packets before transmission.
They encrypt traffic between the browser and the web server.
They read each packet's destination address and forward the packet one step closer to it.

questions.question: What does HTTPS add compared to HTTP?
options: It compresses every request and response to reduce file size.
It caches web pages so the server responds faster on repeat visits.
It encrypts every request and response so an eavesdropper sees only scrambled bytes.
It converts HTML pages into a format that routers can forward more efficiently.

retrieved_chunks:
A computer network connects devices so they can exchange data. A local area network
(LAN) covers a small area such as a home or office; a wide area network (WAN) spans
cities or continents. The internet is a global network of networks: independent
networks agree to exchange traffic using shared protocols, so any connected device can
reach any other.

Data travels across networks in packets. A packet is a small chunk of data — typically
around a kilobyte — carrying headers that record its source address, destination
address, and sequence position. A large file is split into many packets that may take
different routes across the network and arrive out of order; the receiving device
reassembles them into the original data. Packet switching makes networks resilient:
if one route fails, packets flow around the failure.

Every device on the internet has an IP address that identifies it, much as a street
address identifies a building. IPv4 addresses are four numbers between 0 and 255, such
as 192.168.4.12; because IPv4 addresses are running out, the newer IPv6 provides a
vastly larger address space. Routers are devices that read each packet's destination
address and forward the packet one step closer to it. A packet typically crosses many
routers between source and destination.

People remember names, not numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates
human-readable domain names such as example.edu into IP addresses. When a browser
visits a website, it first queries DNS to resolve the name, then connects to the
returned IP address. DNS is a distributed, hierarchical directory — no single server
holds every name.

The World Wide Web runs on top of the internet. A browser requests a page using the
Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP): it sends a request to a web server, and the server
responds with the page content, usually written in HTML. Each request-response pair is
independent, which keeps the protocol simple. URLs identify resources: the scheme
(https), the domain name, and the path together tell the browser what to fetch and how.

Data crossing a network can be intercepted, so sensitive traffic is encrypted. HTTPS
is HTTP protected by encryption: the browser and server agree on keys and encrypt
every request and response, so an eavesdropper sees only scrambled bytes. The padlock
icon in a browser indicates an HTTPS connection. Encryption protects confidentiality
(others cannot read the data) and integrity (tampering is detectable), and
certificates verify that the server is who it claims to be.

An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. A recipe is a
useful analogy: given ingredients (input), following the steps produces a dish
(output). For a procedure to be an algorithm, its steps must be unambiguous, it must
finish after a finite number of steps, and it must produce a correct result for every
valid input. The same algorithm can be expressed in English, in pseudocode, or in any
programming language.

Pseudocode describes an algorithm in structured, language-neutral text. It uses
constructs such as IF/ELSE for decisions, WHILE and FOR for repetition, and variables
for storing values, without the exact syntax of any programming language. Pseudocode
lets people design and discuss an algorithm before writing real code.

Linear search finds a target value in a list by checking each element one at a time,
from the first to the last, until the target is found or the list is exhausted. In the
worst case, linear search examines every element. Its advantage is simplicity: it
works on any list, sorted or not.

Binary search finds a target value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search
range. It compares the target to the middle element: if the target is smaller, the
search continues in the left half; if larger, in the right half. Each comparison
eliminates half the remaining elements, so a list of one million items needs at most
about twenty comparisons. Binary search requires the list to be sorted in advance.

Sorting arranges a list into order. Bubble sort, a simple teaching algorithm,
repeatedly steps through the list and swaps adjacent elements that are out of order;
it is easy to understand but slow on large lists. Merge sort divides the list in half,
sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves; it is dramatically faster on large
inputs. Efficient sorting matters because sorted data enables fast operations like
binary search.

Computer scientists compare algorithms by how their running time grows with input
size, written in Big-O notation. Linear search is O(n): doubling the list doubles the
worst-case work. Binary search is O(log n): doubling a sorted list adds only one more
comparison. Bubble sort is O(n²), while merge sort is O(n log n). For small inputs the
difference barely matters, but at scale the growth rate dominates everything else.

questions.question: What name is given to a computer's working memory that holds running programs and their data?
options: Cache memory
CPU registers
Random access memory (RAM)
Solid-state drive (SSD)

questions.question: According to the storage hierarchy, what happens to RAM's contents when power is removed?
options: They are lost
They are compressed and archived automatically
They are moved to cache memory for safekeeping
They are written to the hard disk drive

questions.question: Which term from the course excerpt directly describes RAM's behavior of losing data when power is removed?
options: Hierarchical
Parallel
Persistent
Volatile

questions.question: Which type of storage retains data WITHOUT power, according to the storage hierarchy?
options: Random access memory (RAM)
Persistent storage (e.g., SSD and HDD)
Cache memory
CPU registers

questions.question: Where does cache memory physically sit within the storage hierarchy?

Inside persistent storage devices

On the motherboard's expansion slots

The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. It repeatedly performs the
fetch-decode-execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it
means, and execute it. CPU speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz), billions of cycles
per second. Modern CPUs contain multiple cores, each capable of executing instructions
independently, which allows a computer to make progress on several tasks at once.

Computers use a hierarchy of storage that trades speed against capacity and cost.
Registers inside the CPU are the fastest and smallest. Cache memory sits next to the
CPU cores and holds recently used data. Random access memory (RAM) is the computer's
working memory: it holds running programs and their data, and its contents are lost
when power is removed — RAM is volatile. Persistent storage — solid-state drives (SSD)
and hard disk drives (HDD) — retains data without power. SSDs use flash memory with no
moving parts and are much faster than HDDs, which store data on spinning magnetic
platters.

The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects every component. Buses are the
communication pathways that carry data between the CPU, memory, and devices. The
chipset manages traffic between components. Expansion slots allow additional cards,
such as a dedicated graphics card, to be added.

Input devices bring data into the computer: keyboards, mice, touchscreens, cameras,
and microphones. Output devices present results: monitors, speakers, and printers.
Ports such as USB provide standardized connections for peripherals. Device drivers are
software components that let the operating system communicate with specific hardware.

The graphics processing unit (GPU) contains thousands of small cores designed to
perform many simple calculations simultaneously. GPUs were created to render images
and video, but their parallel design also makes them well suited to scientific
computing and training machine learning models.

In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip doubled
roughly every two years, an observation known as Moore's law. For decades this drove
exponential growth in computing power at falling cost. In recent years the pace has
slowed as transistors approach physical limits, pushing the industry toward multi-core
designs, specialized chips, and better software efficiency.
